notes:
I've written notes for every verse except 40, 41 and 42a. The section on denominational differences is thin, though. The sources I found mostly agree, and the differences I could document are small. I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or pneumareview.com. The Enduring Word page I opened cut off before verse 29, so its points come only from a search snippet.

## Notes on Luke 8:29–56: the traditional reading

**v. 29:** The Lutheran Kretzmann says that as the Son of God, Jesus had the power, if He so chose, to let the last terrible judgment upon the devils begin at any time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/luke-8.html

**v. 30**
- Constable thinks Jesus asked the demon's name for His disciples' sake. He explains that "Legion" was not a proper name but the name of a Roman military unit that consisted of about 6,000 soldiers. The name "Legion" communicated that thousands of demons indwelt the man. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-31.html
- Guzik (Enduring Word) calls the name evasive, a threat meant to scare. He suggests the demons, like a cornered animal, tried to look bigger in the false hope of frightening Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary suggests the question may have been asked to wake up the man's own buried sense of himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
- Coffman points out that Jesus had already given the command to leave in v. 29 and didn't repeat it. So he disagrees with Barclay's view that Jesus first failed to cast the demon out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-30.html

**v. 31**
- Gill says "the deep" means the bottomless pit, not the sea, since the demons went into the sea of their own accord. They asked not to be sent back to their former prison. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-31.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary links the abyss to the "bottomless pit" of Revelation 9. Vincent notes that Mark records a different request: not to be sent "out of the country." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-31.htm
- Matthew Henry finds comfort here: all the powers of darkness are under Jesus' control. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_008.cfm

**v. 32**
- Guzik says the demons couldn't even afflict pigs without God's permission. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- Bible Hub's study notes compare this to Satan asking permission to test Job and to sift Peter. In both, the Lord sets limits on what demons may do. https://biblehub.com/luke/8-32.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary asks why the demons made this request. It reports Theophylact's idea that they hoped to turn the greedy locals against Jesus by making them fear for their own herds. https://biblehub.com/luke/8-32.htm

**v. 33**
- Guzik: Jesus allowed it so everyone could see what the demons really wanted. They meant to destroy the man just as they destroyed the pigs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-8/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes the usual explanation: the owners deserved the loss because keeping unclean animals broke the Law of Moses. It also gives a different view, that the stampede was a panic that outwitted the demons themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
- Barclay thinks people make too much of the pigs. In his view the man would only believe he was cured if he saw visible proof. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-31.html

**v. 34:** Matthew Henry sees the devil hurting people through their goods, which can tempt them away from Christ. He says Christ allowed it to convince the country what mischief the devil could do in it, if he should suffer him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-36.html

**v. 35:** Guzik, quoted in the Light of Israel commentary: "They were more afraid of a free man than a possessed man." That commentary adds that the people were Gentiles who normally sacrificed pigs, so this was a kind of judgment on their gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-30.html

**v. 36:** Constable says Luke stresses the man's *saving*, the onlookers' fear, and the abyss as the demons' final end. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-31.html

**v. 37**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls "besought Him to depart" one of the saddest sentences in the Gospels. It says the request was probably because of the lost pigs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html
- Constable: the people may have seen Jesus as disturbing, "more interested in saving men than in material prosperity." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-36.html
- Kretzmann: to them the pigs were worth more than the healed man or the Prophet who brought salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/luke-8.html

**v. 38:** The Biblical Illustrator notes that the man's request was the only prayer in the story Jesus refused. The demons and the townspeople both got what they asked. It concludes that some prayers are granted in judgment and some refused in mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-35.html

**v. 39**
- Gill: "how much God has done" quietly hints that Jesus Himself is God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-39.htm
- Constable thinks Luke wants readers to equate what Jesus did with what God did, and says the man "more than obeyed." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-39.html
- The Cambridge Bible: Jesus allowed the news to spread here because He didn't plan to return, so no curious crowds would gather. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-39.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jesus sent him home so he could be a blessing to his country after being a burden to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-39.html

**v. 42b:** Guzik (quoting Clarke): the word for the crowd "pressing" means they almost suffocated Him. It is the same root used for the seed being choked in v. 7. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/luke/luke-8.cfm

**v. 43:** Chuck Smith notes that her bleeding made her ceremonially unclean. She was shut out of worship and cut off from her husband. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-44.html

**v. 44**
- Gill: the "fringe" was the tassel Jews were commanded to wear (Numbers 15:38). She came from behind out of shame. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-44.htm
- Coffman: this doesn't mean Jesus' clothes had magical powers, or that she could be healed without His conscious will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-44.html
- Bible Hub's notes: she was unclean, yet Jesus wasn't defiled by her touch; instead He made her whole. https://biblehub.com/luke/8-44.htm

**vv. 45–46**
- MacLaren says "Who touched Me?" wasn't a sign of ignorance. Jesus asked it to bring her forward to acknowledge what happened. He also contrasts the jostling crowd with the one touch of faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/a-miracle-within-a-miracle.cfm
- MacArthur says Jesus personally felt His power going out to remake her body. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-111/jesus-compassionate-power-part-1

**v. 47:** A sermon on Bible Hub argues that if she had slipped away unseen, she would have left only "half-blessed." She would have been healed, but without knowing His love. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/8-44.htm

**v. 48**
- MacLaren: "Daughter" is the only time Jesus calls a woman this. He taught her that her faith, not her finger, was how the healing reached her. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/a-miracle-within-a-miracle.cfm
- GotQuestions: the Greek word *sozo* means "save" as well as "heal," so her healing was probably spiritual too. https://www.gotquestions.org/your-faith-has-made-you-well.html

**vv. 49–50**
- Matthew Henry: Jesus told Jairus not to doubt His power even though the girl was now dead. Our faith should be bold. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-54.html
- Constable: the woman's interruption tested both Jairus's faith and the disciples' compassion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-44.html
- Bible.org: true faith has hope when all human hope is gone. https://bible.org/seriespage/28-interrupted-miracle-or-two-touching-miracles-luke-840-56

**v. 51:** Constable thinks Jesus let in only a few, perhaps because the room was small or to spare the girl attention. More importantly, He wanted to avoid publicity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html

**v. 52**
- Gill: the mourners included hired mourning women. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html
- Matthew Henry: "sleep" means she wasn't dead for good. She would soon be raised, as if she had only slept a few hours. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html
- The Cambridge Bible: taking "asleep" literally goes against the whole story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-52.htm

**v. 53:** Henry: the mockers' certainty that she was dead actually proves the miracle was real. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html

**v. 54:** Chuck Smith says the Greek for "Child" means "my little child." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html

**v. 55**
- R.C. Sproul: "her spirit returned" shows this was a resurrection, not reviving someone in a coma. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/jairus-daughter-luk51
- The Biblical Illustrator says the meal proved the miracle was real and complete. It also shows she was raised to ordinary life, unlike the final resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html
- Matthew Henry treats the food as a picture: people newly raised from sin hunger for spiritual food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/8-52.htm

**v. 56:** Constable: Jesus wanted to avoid the publicity a second raising would bring (compare Luke 7:11–17). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html

## Where traditions differ

**v. 44: was her faith superstitious?**
- MacLaren (Baptist) calls her faith "very ignorant," because she expected a physical touch to heal her. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/a-miracle-within-a-miracle.cfm
- Guzik says her faith had some error and superstition, but the cloak served as a "point of contact." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/luke/luke-8.cfm
- MacArthur says This is not superstition. This is faith in the power of Jesus. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-111/jesus-compassionate-power-part-1

**v. 52: what "asleep" means**
- Sproul (Reformed) says Jesus wasn't teaching "soul sleep." He calls that a heresy and says "asleep" was a common Jewish euphemism. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/jairus-daughter-luk51
- Wesley's Notes (Arminian) explain that her soul was not finally separated from her body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html

**v. 48: does faith guarantee healing?**
- Seedbed (Wesleyan) says Jesus was stressing trust and not giving up. He was not to create an eternal metric for why a healing does or does not occur. https://seedbed.com/att-when-to-say-your-faith-has-healed-you/
- GotQuestions agrees: healing depends on the Healer, not on how good one's faith is. https://www.gotquestions.org/your-faith-has-made-you-well.html
- Neither page names prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, and I found no page that describes that teaching directly.

**v. 39:** The Lutheran site 1517.org applies the man's sending to believers' witness today. https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-826-39-pentecost-2-series-c

## Other views

**Barclay (vv. 31–33, 52)**
- He frames the demons in terms of the people's strong belief in demons. On this view it was the man who pleaded, *thinking* demons were speaking through him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-31.html
- He also suggests the girl may literally have been in a deep trance, about to be buried alive. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/8-52.html
- Others reject both ideas: Coffman (v. 30), the Cambridge Bible and Sproul (v. 52).

**Church fathers (the Catena Aurea, a medieval Catholic collection)**
- Augustine works through the apparent conflict with Matthew, who says the girl was already dead when Jairus came.
- The Catena says her spirit returning means He restored her own soul, not a different one.
- Theophylact reads it as a picture: as the Church was cleansed (the woman), the Synagogue died through unbelief (the girl).

Source: https://www.studylight.org/bible/arc/pes/luke/8-55.html
